entries.title: How can an idea become a federal law?
entries.answer: A member of Congress can put an idea into a written proposal called a bill. A small group in the House or Senate can study it, hear from people, and suggest changes. For an ordinary bill to pass, both chambers must agree to the same words. The bill then typically goes to the president. A president can sign it or veto it, and other outcomes depend on timing and what Congress does. Many bills never pass all of these steps.
facts: Two different versions of a bill must be worked into the same final text before it can go to the president.

entries.title: How did the Thirteenth Amendment change the Constitution?
entries.answer: The Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery and forced labor across the United States, except as punishment after conviction for a crime. States approved it in 1865, when the Civil War was ending. It was broader than the earlier Emancipation Proclamation, which applied to certain areas still in rebellion. Ending slavery did not settle all questions about citizenship, voting, or fair treatment. Two later amendments during Reconstruction addressed other parts of those problems.
facts: The amendment gives Congress power to enforce it by passing laws.

entries.title: What are the three branches of the U.S. government?
entries.answer: The United States divides federal government work among three branches. The legislative branch, Congress, makes federal laws. The executive branch, led by the president, carries out those laws. The judicial branch includes the federal courts, which decide cases and interpret laws. Each branch has some ways to check the power of another. A president can reject a bill passed by Congress, for example, but Congress can still pass it if enough lawmakers in both parts vote to override that decision.
facts: Congress is part of the legislative branch.
The Supreme Court is part of the judicial branch.

entries.title: What barriers did the Voting Rights Act of 1965 address?
entries.answer: Even after the Constitution banned certain racial barriers to voting, officials in many places found ways to keep Black citizens from registering. Some required unfair tests or used confusing paperwork. People organized, marched, and called attention to those barriers. In 1965 Congress passed the Voting Rights Act. It blocked practices such as those tests in covered places and gave the national government tools to help enforce voting rights. The law mattered because rights on paper are hard to use when officials can stop people at the door.
facts: The Civil Rights Act and Voting Rights Act were signed in successive years.

entries.title: What can a town decide at a town meeting?
entries.answer: In some towns, a town meeting makes certain local decisions. People might talk about how much the town should spend or whether a town rule needs to change. An open meeting can let registered town voters vote for themselves. Other towns elect representatives who do the voting at the meeting. A moderator helps the meeting follow its rules while people speak and vote. The meeting’s work depends on state law and how the town is organized.
facts: Massachusetts has towns with both open and representative town meetings.

entries.title: What did the Civil Rights Act of 1964 change?
entries.answer: People fighting unfair treatment in the United States had organized, protested, and gone to court for years. In 1964 Congress passed a law to ban certain kinds of discrimination. For example, many hotels and restaurants could no longer refuse people because of race. The law also addressed unequal treatment in many workplaces and gave the federal government ways to enforce protections. The Civil Rights Act was part of a wider effort to make public life open to more people.
facts: President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act into law in July 1964.

entries.title: What do state and local governments do?
entries.answer: In the United States, states make many rules for people and organizations within their state. Cities, towns, and counties may handle work that affects smaller places, such as collecting trash or taking care of local streets. The exact work depends on the state and the community. A school board, city council, or county office might decide different things. In many places voters choose some of these local officials. Other people are hired or appointed to do work for the community.
facts: Depending on where you live, local elections can include city, county, or school offices.

entries.title: What does a jury do in a trial?
entries.answer: A trial jury is a small group of people chosen to hear testimony and look at evidence in a court case. The judge tells them what legal rules to use. In a typical jury trial, the group discusses the facts and gives a decision called a verdict. Some trial juries decide whether a person has been proved guilty of a crime. Others settle disputes between people or organizations. Courts can also decide many cases without a jury.
facts: In the federal system, a grand jury asks a different question from a trial jury, about whether a criminal charge can go forward.

entries.title: What does federalism mean in the United States?
entries.answer: Federalism means that governing power is divided between the national government and the states. The U.S. Constitution gives the national government powers such as making rules for trade across state borders. States have their own governments and make many of the rules people use close to home. For example, they issue driver’s licenses. Some responsibilities overlap, and both levels can collect taxes. The Constitution sets rules that help people decide which level of government may act when there is a disagreement.
facts: The Tenth Amendment deals with powers reserved to the states or to the people.
National and state governments each have their own lawmakers.

entries.title: What does it mean to become a citizen by naturalization?
entries.answer: A citizen is someone recognized as a member of a country under its laws. Some people are citizens at birth. A person who becomes a citizen after birth can sometimes do so through a legal process called naturalization. In the United States the process can include an application, an interview, and an oath at a ceremony. Different rules can apply to people with different histories. New citizens can take part in civic life and may vote if they meet the voting rules.
facts: Naturalization and citizenship at birth are different ways a person can become a citizen.

entries.title: What does the Fourteenth Amendment say about citizenship?
entries.answer: The Fourteenth Amendment says that people born or naturalized in the United States and under its authority are citizens. It also says states cannot take away certain rights without proper legal steps or deny anyone the equal protection of the laws. States approved it in 1868, when the country was dealing with the effects of slavery and the Civil War. The wording about fairness later mattered in court cases well beyond those first years.
facts: The Supreme Court used the amendment’s equal protection rule in Brown v. Board of Education.

entries.title: What does the United States Supreme Court do?
entries.answer: The Supreme Court is the highest court in the federal court system. It reviews selected cases that raise important questions about federal law or the Constitution. Lawyers explain the issues and judges discuss and decide the case. The Court often writes an opinion spelling out why it reached a decision. Those opinions can guide how lower courts decide similar cases. Most trials, witnesses, and juries are found in other courts, long before a case might reach the Supreme Court.
facts: The judges of the Supreme Court are called justices.

entries.title: What does the Universal Declaration of Human Rights say?
entries.answer: In 1948, representatives at the United Nations agreed on a statement about basic rights that people everywhere should have. It describes freedoms and protections that belong to people because they are human. The statement includes ideas about safety, fair treatment, education, and the ability to share beliefs. It sets out goals and principles rather than a set of rules enforced by one world government. Later laws and treaties have drawn on it in different ways.
facts: The declaration says that all people are born free and equal in dignity and rights.

entries.title: What happens to ballots in an election?
entries.answer: Officials set up an election so eligible voters can choose among candidates or answer questions on a ballot. Depending on where they live, people might vote at a voting place or return a ballot by mail. After people have voted, election workers count valid ballots and check records. They may compare totals, review ballots whose choices are unclear, and perform other required checks. Officials announce and confirm results after following the rules for that election, which can differ by state.
facts: In the United States, many elections are run by local officials under state rules.

entries.title: What happens when the president vetoes a bill?
entries.answer: If a president disagrees with a bill passed by Congress, the president can send it back with objections. That is called a veto. The bill normally will not become law at that point. But Congress can vote again. If two-thirds of the members voting in each chamber support overriding the veto, the bill can become law anyway. The rule means a president can make it harder for a bill to pass, while a large enough group of lawmakers can still pass it.
facts: A successful veto override needs enough votes in both the House and Senate.

entries.title: What is the Electoral College?
entries.answer: When people vote for president of the United States, their votes help decide which group of electors their state will pick. Those electors cast formal votes for president and vice president later. States have different numbers of electors based on their representation in Congress, and the District of Columbia also has electors. In most states the winning candidate gets all of that state’s electoral votes. A candidate needs more than half of the electoral votes to win in the usual process.
facts: The Electoral College has 538 elector positions under the present allocation.

entries.title: What is the U.S. Bill of Rights?
entries.answer: The Bill of Rights is the name for the first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution. An amendment adds to or changes a rule in the Constitution. The First Amendment protects freedoms that include religion, speech, and the right to gather peacefully. Other amendments set rules about searches and how people are treated in court. These protections put limits on government power. People sometimes disagree about how the words apply to a new situation, so courts may have to decide what the protections require.
facts: The first ten amendments were approved by enough states to take effect in 1791.
Congress originally proposed twelve amendments in this group.

entries.title: What is the U.S. Congress?
entries.answer: Congress is the part of the United States government that makes federal laws. It has two parts, called the House of Representatives and the Senate. Every state has two senators. States with more people usually have more seats in the House than states with fewer people. Members in both parts study problems, talk about ideas for laws, and vote. To send a bill to the president, the House and Senate generally must agree to the same words in it.
facts: The Senate gives each state two seats.
House seats are redistributed among states using results of the census.

entries.title: What is the U.S. Constitution?
entries.answer: The U.S. Constitution sets the basic rules for the United States government. It says what the different branches of the federal government may do and sets limits on their power. Delegates met in Philadelphia in 1787 to write it. Afterward, states held meetings to decide whether to approve it. The Constitution can be changed by adding amendments. A person trying to understand the rules today needs to look at the original document and the amendments together.
facts: The U.S. Constitution was signed in Philadelphia in 1787.
Article V describes how the Constitution can be amended.

entries.title: What voting rule did the Fifteenth Amendment add?
entries.answer: The Fifteenth Amendment says the United States and states cannot deny or reduce voting rights on account of race, color, or having been enslaved. States approved it in 1870. In practice, many officials later used unfair tests, intimidation, and other barriers to stop Black citizens from voting. The amendment did not remove rules that kept most women from voting in many places. Later amendments and laws made other changes to protect access to the ballot.
facts: The amendment also says Congress can pass laws to enforce it.

entries.title: Why do different parts of the US government check one another?
entries.answer: The Constitution gives different kinds of work to Congress, the president, and the courts. It also gives one branch ways to limit or review actions taken by another. The president can veto a bill Congress passed. Congress can override a veto with enough votes. Federal courts can decide in cases whether a law fits the Constitution. These rules are called checks and balances. They can slow down a decision and make different parts of government explain or reconsider what they are doing.
facts: The Senate votes on whether to confirm many people nominated by the president, including nominees for federal judges.

entries.title: Why does the United States take a census?
entries.answer: A census counts the people who live in a place. The United States takes a census of the whole country once every ten years. One reason is to figure out how to divide seats in the House of Representatives among the states. Population changes can make a state gain or lose seats after a census. Census numbers also help communities plan. If many more children live in an area than before, for example, planners can use population information while thinking about schools and other services.
facts: The first U.S. census took place in 1790.
The 50 states’ population counts are used to divide House seats.

entries.title: Why were the Federalist Papers written?
entries.answer: After delegates proposed the Constitution in 1787, the states had to decide whether to approve it. Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay wrote essays to persuade people to support the plan. They published them under one name, Publius. The essays explained why the writers wanted a stronger national government and how they expected its powers to be limited. Other writers disagreed. These arguments let us read some of the discussion that happened between writing the Constitution and putting it into use.
facts: The collection includes eighty-five essays.
